title: Respiratory System
tagline: Breathing and gas exchange, lung function, asthma and COPD, infections, lung cancer and respiratory failure
summary: Breathing delivers oxygen and removes carbon dioxide, and failure of either quickly becomes dangerous. This course covers the mechanics of breathing, gas exchange and its control, lung function tests, and the main diseases of the lungs: asthma and COPD, respiratory infections including tuberculosis, interstitial and pulmonary vascular disease, lung cancer and pleural disease, and respiratory failure.
overview: The respiratory system has two physical jobs: moving air in and out of the lungs, and moving oxygen and carbon dioxide across the thin barrier between air and blood. A control system in the brainstem adjusts ventilation to keep arterial carbon dioxide and oxygen near their set points. This course builds that framework first, because asthma, COPD, fibrosis, pulmonary embolism and respiratory failure can each be understood as a failure of one of its parts.

The first three chapters cover the physiology: pressures, lung volumes, compliance, surfactant, airway resistance and the limit on expiratory flow; diffusion, ventilation–perfusion matching, the alveolar gas equation and the A–a gradient, and the carriage of oxygen and carbon dioxide; the chemoreceptors and the control of breathing, sleep-disordered breathing, and the interpretation of spirometry, lung volumes, gas transfer and blood gases. The clinical chapters then apply the framework: asthma and COPD; pneumonia, influenza, COVID-19 and tuberculosis; interstitial lung disease, pulmonary embolism and pulmonary hypertension; lung cancer and pleural disease; and respiratory failure, with oxygen therapy, non-invasive ventilation and lung-protective ventilation.

Calculations recur throughout: compliance, A–a gradients from real blood gases, oxygen content, shunt and dead space fractions, compensation in acid–base disorders, severity scores, predicted postoperative lung function and ventilator tidal volumes. Worked cases take each calculation from raw numbers to a clinical decision. Management is described as principle under current guidance, mainly UK sources (NICE, BTS, SIGN) alongside international reports such as GINA, GOLD and the ESC/ERS guidelines, and is not advice for individual patients.
outcomes: Explain the mechanics of breathing: respiratory pressures, lung volumes and their measurement, compliance and surfactant, airway resistance, dynamic compression and the work of breathing.
Interpret spirometry, flow–volume loops, lung volumes and gas transfer to distinguish obstructive, restrictive and pulmonary vascular patterns, using reference values and the lower limit of normal.
Use the alveolar gas equation to calculate the A–a gradient, and explain the five causes of hypoxaemia, the oxygen–haemoglobin dissociation curve and the transport of carbon dioxide.
Explain the control of breathing by central and peripheral chemoreceptors, and the mechanisms of opioid-induced hypoventilation, oxygen-induced hypercapnia and obstructive sleep apnoea.
Interpret arterial blood gases systematically, including compensation in acute and chronic respiratory acidosis.

Describe the pathophysiology, diagnosis and stepwise management principles of asthma and COPD, including acute severe asthma and exacerbations of COPD, in line with current UK and international guidance.
Classify pneumonia by setting, assess severity with CRB65 and CURB65, outline antibiotic principles and recognise complications, and describe influenza, COVID-19 and tuberculosis.
Describe the main interstitial lung diseases, including idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, hypersensitivity pneumonitis and sarcoidosis, and their investigation and treatment principles.
Outline the diagnosis and management of pulmonary embolism, and define and classify pulmonary hypertension.
Classify lung cancer, describe its presentation, staging and treatment principles, and manage pleural effusion and pneumothorax in line with current guidance.
Define type 1 and type 2 respiratory failure and explain the principles of oxygen therapy, CPAP, non-invasive ventilation, invasive ventilation and lung-protective ventilation in ARDS.

history.title: The vital capacity
history.detail: John Hutchinson, a London physician, publishes spirometer measurements from about 2,000 people. He names the vital capacity, shows that it rises with height and notes that it falls in disease.

history.title: The tubercle bacillus
history.detail: Robert Koch announces in Berlin on 24 March that he has identified the bacillus that causes tuberculosis. The date is now marked as World TB Day.

history.title: Diffusion, not secretion
history.detail: August and Marie Krogh show by careful measurement that passive diffusion can account for oxygen uptake in the lung, settling a long dispute with Christian Bohr and John Scott Haldane, who believed the lung actively secreted oxygen.

history.title: Streptomycin for tuberculosis
history.detail: The British Medical Research Council publishes its trial of streptomycin in pulmonary tuberculosis, one of the first randomised controlled trials. It and later trials show that resistance emerges with a single drug, establishing combination therapy.

history.title: Smoking and lung cancer
history.detail: Richard Doll and Austin Bradford Hill in Britain, and Ernst Wynder and Evarts Graham in the United States, publish case–control studies showing a strong association between cigarette smoking and lung cancer.

history.title: The Copenhagen polio epidemic
history.detail: Overwhelmed by patients with respiratory paralysis, the Blegdam Hospital adopts Bjørn Ibsen's proposal of tracheostomy and manual positive-pressure ventilation by relays of students. Mortality falls sharply, and the epidemic leads to the first intensive care units.

history.title: Surfactant deficiency in the newborn
history.detail: Building on the work of Richard Pattle and John Clements on the surface-active lining of the lung, Mary Ellen Avery and Jere Mead show that babies who died of hyaline membrane disease lacked surfactant, the basis of later surfactant therapy.

history.title: Acute respiratory distress in adults
history.detail: David Ashbaugh, Thomas Petty and colleagues describe in The Lancet a syndrome of acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure in adults with stiff lungs and bilateral infiltrates, later called ARDS.

history.title: The natural history of airflow obstruction
history.detail: Charles Fletcher and Richard Peto show that only susceptible smokers lose lung function rapidly, and that stopping smoking returns the rate of decline towards normal.

history.title: Lung-protective ventilation
history.detail: The ARDS Network trial shows that ventilating patients with ARDS using low tidal volumes (6 mL/kg predicted body weight) reduces mortality compared with traditional volumes.
